summary: A small delegation sent to St. Louis to secure release of a Sauk man held for murder signed a cession of a huge area between the Mississippi and Illinois rivers. summary: Ratification required signatures of three-fourths of Ute adult men. Most Uncompahgre and Southern Utes refused; Ouray died in Aug 1880 without signing the ratification (per Conetah). Commissioner Otto Mears then paid Ute men two dollars per signature. Chairman Manypenny refused to approve and Mears was ordered to Washington, but Secretary Kirkwood dropped charges and reimbursed Mears for the bribes.

summary: Fred Conetah's history of the Northern Ute (1982), as quoted by PSL TREC, states that commissioner Otto Mears paid Utes $2 each to sign the 1880 agreement. The Ute Commission's report counts 581 adult male signatures given 'without restraint' and does not mention payments.

quote: The Indian loss in this fight is said to be one man, two small girls, and an infant boy killed
summary: In August 1887 a Colorado posse burned Colorow's hunting camp, and militia and posse then attacked the camp at dawn near the Utah reservation line, killing one man, two small girls and an infant boy, the Commissioner of Indian Affairs reported. The Utes lost over 600 horses and about 2,500 sheep and goats.

quote: We examined the land on the Grand River near the mouth of the Gunnison, and found it to be, in our opinion, unsuit- able for the Indians for agricultural or grazing purposes.
summary: The 1880 agreement promised the Uncompahgre land on the Grand River near the Gunnison if enough farmland existed there, otherwise in Utah. The commissioners judged it unsuitable and moved them to Utah. PSL TREC says the report was false; the later ICC claim (Docket 349) was settled for $300,000 without a finding.

citation: United States v. Southern Ute Indians, 402 U.S. 159, 160-161 and n. 2 (1971); 117 Ct. Cl. 433, 436 (1950)
quote: We therefore hold that the claim in this case is res judicata under the 1950 consent judgment enforcing the settlement agreement
summary: Court of Claims consent judgments in 1950 (Case No. 46640) were entered as 'full settlement and payment for the complete extinguishment' of Ute title to the western Colorado land ceded under the 1880 act; the settlements exceeded $31 million (United States v. Southern Ute, 1971). Money, not land, closed the claim.

quote: With the massacre in mind, Congress decided to remove the Indians from the Colorado reservation as part of the punishment meted out for this tragedy.
summary: After the 1879 Meeker/Milk Creek fighting, Congress used the 1880 Act to punish the Utes and remove them from Colorado, barring payments until the participants surrendered and deducting victims' compensation from land proceeds. The Uncompahgre were removed too though they had no role in the incident.

The 1868 treaty reserved western Colorado for the Utes, and the 1880 agreement left this strip to the Southern Utes. The Hunter Act of 1895 then opened the land not allotted to entry 'under the desert, homestead, and town-site laws', while the Weeminuche moved to the western end. This happened after Royce's 1894 cutoff.

quote: the claim in this case is res judicata under the 1950 consent judgment
summary: The ICC (1966) held the Southern Utes entitled to compensation for 230,547.44 acres disposed of under the 1895 Act and an accounting incl. 81,953.18 more acres; it found (1969) Royce 617 was never intended in the 1950 Confederated Ute settlement. The Supreme Court in 1971 held the claim res judicata under the 1950 consent judgment, ruling the 1880 Act ceded all non-allotted land; Docket 328 barred July 14, 1971.

quote: Uncompahgre Indians have no title to any of the lands within the [Uncompahgre] reservation [and] nothing more than the privilege of temporary occupancy.
summary: In 1894 Congress declared the Uncompahgre had 'no title' and only temporary occupancy. The 1897 Act opened unallotted lands; only 83 allotments were made. The ICC settled Docket 349 for $300,000 barring further claims, yet the Tenth Circuit holds the reservation boundary intact, and Interior (Jorjani 2018) denied restoring the land.

summary: The Northern Cheyenne had no reservation of their own until the executive order of Nov. 26, 1884, about 16 years after the 1868 treaty. The order excluded tracts already held by white settlers and left Tongue River families outside its line. Congress made the reservation tribal property only in 1926.

summary: The 1832 and 1833 treaties promised the Creeks a 'permanent home' with a fee patent (issued 1852). The 1866 treaty took the western half (486/698); allotment followed. McGirt held the 1866 reservation was never disestablished.
